title: Dr. Patel's Clinic: Diagnosis Challenge
theme: Medical Diagnosis in a Rural Indian Clinic
description: You are Dr. Meera Patel, a young MBBS doctor posted at a Primary Health Centre (PHC) in a small village in Gujarat under the National Rural Health Mission. With limited equipment, a tight budget, and patients who have walked hours to see you, every decision matters. Diagnose mysterious symptoms, order the right tests within budget, treat patients with the resources available, and learn when to refer to a district hospital. Your patient's health, your budget, diagnostic accuracy, and precious time are all in your hands. Welcome to the reality of rural Indian healthcare.
learning_objectives: Understand the structure of India's public healthcare system (PHC, CHC, District Hospital)
Learn basic medical reasoning: symptoms, differential diagnosis, and treatment approaches
Appreciate the challenges of rural healthcare in India including resource constraints and access issues
Understand the importance of preventive medicine, vaccination, and public health
Develop decision-making skills under resource constraints and time pressure

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: You are Dr. Meera Patel running a Primary Health Centre in rural Gujarat
Each round presents a patient with symptoms that you must evaluate and treat
Choose from different diagnostic approaches, tests, and treatment options
Monitor Patient Health, Budget (INR), Accuracy, and Time as you make decisions
Budget is limited -- expensive tests may be accurate but drain your resources for other patients
Some patients need referral to a district hospital; recognizing when is a crucial skill
tips: Listen to symptoms carefully -- the most obvious diagnosis is not always correct
Expensive tests are not always necessary; clinical examination can reveal a lot
Budget management is critical -- you serve an entire village, not just one patient
Time matters; some conditions are emergencies while others can wait
Preventive advice and public health education save more lives than any single treatment

rounds.title: Round 1: The Feverish Child
rounds.story: Your first patient is 6-year-old Raju, brought in by his worried mother Kamala. He has had a high fever (103 F) for three days, headache, body aches, and a faint rash on his arms. Kamala says there are many mosquitoes near their house and the village pond has stagnant water. Raju's village is in a known dengue-endemic area, but malaria is also common in the region. Your PHC has a rapid malaria test kit, a basic blood testing facility, and standard medications. Kamala cannot afford private hospital fees.
rounds.goal: Diagnose the cause of Raju's fever using available resources and decide on the appropriate treatment.

choices.label: Use Rapid Diagnostic Test for Malaria + Dengue NS1
choices.feedback: The rapid diagnostic test (RDT) takes just 15 minutes. Raju tests negative for malaria but positive for Dengue NS1 antigen. Dengue is caused by the Aedes aegypti mosquito, which breeds in clean stagnant water. India reports lakhs of dengue cases annually, with major outbreaks during post-monsoon season. RDTs are cost-effective tools that have revolutionized diagnosis in resource-limited settings under the National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP).

choices.label: Rely on Clinical Examination Only (Save Budget)
choices.feedback: You examine Raju thoroughly -- the rash pattern, tourniquet test, and symptom timeline suggest dengue, but you cannot be certain without lab confirmation. Clinical diagnosis saves money but risks missing co-infections or misidentifying the disease. In rural India, where lab facilities are limited, clinical skills are essential. However, the ICMR guidelines recommend laboratory confirmation for vector-borne diseases whenever possible to ensure correct treatment.

choices.label: Order Complete Blood Count + Liver Function Test
choices.feedback: The CBC shows low platelet count (thrombocytopenia) and elevated liver enzymes -- classic dengue indicators. You can now grade the severity and monitor for dengue hemorrhagic fever. While more expensive, the comprehensive blood work gives you a complete picture. India's public health labs under the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) are designed to provide such testing, but equipment and staffing remain challenges at PHC level.

rounds.coaching_moment: Consider how this choice affects your long-term resources, not just the immediate gain.

rounds.title: Round 2: The Pregnant Woman's Dilemma
rounds.story: Savitaben, 28, is seven months pregnant and has come for a routine check-up. She appears pale and tired. Her haemoglobin is only 7 g/dL -- severe anaemia. She admits she has not been taking the iron-folic acid tablets distributed by the ASHA worker because they cause nausea. Her blood pressure is also mildly elevated. The nearest district hospital with a blood bank is 80 kilometres away. The village has no ambulance, and the road is unpaved. Savitaben says she wants to deliver at home with a traditional midwife, as her mother and grandmother did.
rounds.goal: Manage Savitaben's anaemia and high-risk pregnancy while respecting her preferences and working within your constraints.

choices.label: Strongly Recommend District Hospital Transfer Now
choices.feedback: You explain the risks of severe anaemia during delivery: postpartum hemorrhage is the leading cause of maternal death in India. Under the Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY), Savitaben is entitled to free institutional delivery and a cash incentive. You arrange a 108 ambulance service call. India's Maternal Mortality Rate has improved dramatically (from 556 in 1990 to 97 in 2020) largely due to institutional deliveries. Referring high-risk pregnancies saves lives.

choices.label: Treat Anaemia Aggressively at PHC + Monitor
choices.feedback: You start IV iron sucrose therapy (available at your PHC) and prescribe a different formulation of oral iron that causes less nausea. You schedule weekly monitoring. The ASHA worker will do daily home visits. India's anaemia burden is enormous -- over 50% of pregnant women are anaemic (NFHS-5 data). The National Iron Plus Initiative provides free supplements, but adherence remains a challenge. Your local treatment keeps her close to family but requires careful monitoring.

choices.label: Counsel on Diet + Modified Iron Supplements + Birth Plan
choices.feedback: You counsel Savitaben on iron-rich foods locally available: jaggery (gud), green leafy vegetables (palak, methi), dates, and sprouted pulses. You switch her to a slow-release iron formulation taken with orange juice (vitamin C aids absorption). You create a birth plan with the ASHA worker. Nutrition education is a cornerstone of India's POSHAN Abhiyaan (National Nutrition Mission). Empowering patients with knowledge about locally available nutrition is often the most sustainable solution.

rounds.title: Round 3: The Mystery Rash
rounds.story: Twelve children from the village school arrive at your PHC with an itchy rash, mild fever, and swollen lymph nodes. The school teacher is panicking, parents are gathering outside, and rumours are flying that it might be a dangerous epidemic. Some parents want to take their children to a private clinic in the nearest town. Your ASHA worker reports that the symptoms started three days ago with just two children and have been spreading. The rash appears as small red spots that started on the face and spread downward.
rounds.goal: Identify the outbreak, manage community panic, and implement appropriate public health measures.

choices.label: Suspect Measles -- Check Vaccination Records
choices.feedback: You check the children's vaccination records and find that 8 of the 12 missed their second dose of MMR vaccine. The rash pattern (maculopapular, starting from face, moving downward) with Koplik's spots inside the cheeks confirms measles. India's Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP) provides free vaccines, but coverage gaps persist in rural areas. The WHO estimates that measles vaccination has prevented over 56 million deaths globally since 2000. Your quick identification prevents further spread.

choices.label: Isolate Affected Children + Alert District Health Officer
choices.feedback: You immediately separate the affected children and call the District Surveillance Unit under IDSP (Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme). Outbreak investigation teams have protocols for exactly this situation. India's disease surveillance system improved dramatically after the 2009 H1N1 pandemic. Rapid reporting through the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP) helps track outbreaks in real-time. Your quick action prevents the outbreak from becoming an epidemic.

choices.label: Hold a Community Meeting to Calm Fears + Educate
choices.feedback: You gather the parents and explain the situation calmly. You use this as an opportunity to discuss the importance of completing the vaccination schedule. Many parents did not know about the second dose. Community health education is a fundamental principle of India's National Health Policy. The ASHA worker programme -- with nearly 10 lakh workers across India -- was designed precisely for this bridge between medical knowledge and community understanding. Education prevents the next outbreak.

rounds.title: Round 4: The Snakebite Emergency
rounds.story: A farmer named Bhikhabhai is rushed in by his family on a bullock cart. He was bitten by a snake while working in his field 45 minutes ago. His foot is swelling rapidly, and he is showing signs of pain and anxiety. The family did not see the snake clearly but describe it as 'dark and thick.' They have tied a tight tourniquet above the bite and applied a paste of herbs -- both harmful practices. Your PHC has polyvalent anti-snake venom (ASV), but you need to assess the envenomation severity quickly. The nearest ICU is 2 hours away.
rounds.goal: Manage this snakebite emergency with limited resources while correcting harmful first-aid practices.

choices.label: Remove Tourniquet + Start Anti-Snake Venom Immediately
choices.feedback: You immediately remove the dangerous tourniquet (it can cause tissue death) and wash off the herbal paste. You start IV ASV while monitoring for anaphylaxis. India has the highest snakebite deaths in the world -- over 50,000 annually. The WHO lists snakebite as a Neglected Tropical Disease. Polyvalent ASV, made by Indian manufacturers like Haffkine Institute, covers the Big Four: cobra, krait, Russell's viper, and saw-scaled viper. Your quick, protocol-based response saves Bhikhabhai's life.

choices.label: Assess Envenomation Grade Before Deciding on ASV
choices.feedback: You use the 20-minute Whole Blood Clotting Test (20WBCT) -- a simple bedside test to check for coagulopathy. If blood does not clot in 20 minutes, it indicates viper envenomation requiring ASV. This test, recommended by WHO and India's National Snakebite Protocol, saves expensive ASV for cases that truly need it. Not every snakebite requires ASV (30-50% are dry bites). Careful assessment prevents both under-treatment and wasteful over-treatment in a resource-limited setting.

choices.label: Give First Aid + Immediately Refer to District Hospital
choices.feedback: You immobilize the limb, start IV fluids, and arrange emergency transport. However, the 2-hour journey to the district hospital is risky for a snakebite patient. Every PHC in snake-endemic areas should be equipped and trained to administer ASV. India's National Health Mission mandates ASV availability at all PHCs in high-risk districts. Referral is sometimes necessary but delaying ASV in a confirmed envenomation can be fatal -- the golden hour matters in snakebite management.

rounds.title: Round 5: The Silent Epidemic -- Diabetes Screening
rounds.story: During a routine health camp organized with the ASHA worker network, you screen 50 adults from the village for blood sugar levels. The results are alarming: 12 people (24%) have blood sugar levels above normal, and 5 of them are clearly diabetic but have never been diagnosed. Most are between 35-55 years old, and many are surprised because they feel fine. India is the 'Diabetes Capital of the World' with over 77 million diabetics. You must decide how to use your limited budget and time to address this public health crisis.
rounds.goal: Design an effective diabetes management strategy for the village within the constraints of your rural PHC.

choices.label: Set Up Individual Treatment Plans for All 12 Patients
choices.feedback: You prescribe medication (Metformin for confirmed diabetics), schedule regular follow-ups, and counsel each patient individually on diet and exercise. The cost is significant but necessary. India's Ayushman Bharat scheme aims to provide comprehensive primary healthcare including diabetes management at Health and Wellness Centres. Individual treatment is gold standard but unsustainable without systemic support. You are treating the current patients but not preventing new ones.

choices.label: Launch a Village-Wide Diabetes Prevention Programme
choices.feedback: You organize daily walking groups, partner with the local anganwadi for nutrition education, and train ASHA workers to conduct monthly screening camps. Prevention is more cost-effective than treatment. India's National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke (NPCDCS) focuses on exactly this approach. Lifestyle changes can prevent up to 80% of Type 2 diabetes cases. Your community programme reaches more people than individual treatment ever could.

choices.label: Focus on Local Diet Modification Education
choices.feedback: You explain that traditional Indian diets (millets like bajra and jowar, dal, vegetables) are actually healthier than modern processed food. The shift from millets to polished rice and wheat, increased sugar consumption, and sedentary lifestyles are driving India's diabetes epidemic. You promote the government's Millet Mission and local food over packaged snacks. This low-cost intervention addresses the root cause. India's millet-based traditional diets, recognized by the UN as International Year of Millets (2023), are naturally low-glycemic and diabetes-preventive.

rounds.title: Round 6: The Mental Health Crisis
rounds.story: A farmer's wife, Jashiben, comes to you complaining of persistent headaches, body pain, and inability to sleep. Physical examination reveals nothing abnormal. After gentle questioning, she breaks down crying. Her husband has been depressed since crop failure last season and has stopped working. The family is in debt to a moneylender. She fears he might harm himself. Mental health in rural India is severely under-addressed -- there is no psychiatrist within 100 kilometres of your PHC. The stigma around mental illness is enormous in the village.
rounds.goal: Address a mental health crisis in a setting with virtually no mental health infrastructure and significant social stigma.

choices.label: Arrange Tele-Psychiatry Consultation via e-Sanjeevani
choices.feedback: India's e-Sanjeevani telemedicine platform, launched under Ayushman Bharat, connects rural PHCs with specialists. You arrange a tele-consultation with a psychiatrist at the district hospital. The psychiatrist assesses the husband for clinical depression and prescribes medication that you can dispense at the PHC. India has only 0.3 psychiatrists per 100,000 people (vs. WHO recommendation of 1). Telemedicine is bridging this gap -- e-Sanjeevani has facilitated crores of teleconsultations across India.

choices.label: Mobilize Community Support + Address Financial Stress
choices.feedback: You connect the family with the Kisan Samman Nidhi scheme and crop insurance claims through the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana. You also speak with the village sarpanch about creating a farmer support group. India loses a farmer to suicide every 30 minutes, often driven by debt and crop failure. The District Mental Health Programme (DMHP) under the National Mental Health Policy aims to integrate mental health into primary care. Addressing financial stress is often the first step in treating farmer depression.

choices.label: Train ASHA Worker in Basic Mental Health First Aid
choices.feedback: You spend time training your ASHA worker to recognize signs of depression, suicidal ideation, and anxiety using NIMHANS-developed screening tools. The ASHA worker can visit the family daily and report any warning signs. India's Mental Healthcare Act (2017) recognizes the right to mental health care as a fundamental right. Task-shifting mental health screening to community health workers is a WHO-recommended strategy for countries with limited psychiatric resources. One trained ASHA worker can monitor dozens of at-risk families.

rounds.title: Round 7: The Water-Borne Outbreak
rounds.story: After heavy monsoon rains, 30 villagers present with severe diarrhoea, vomiting, and dehydration over two days. Your PHC is overwhelmed. The village water supply -- an open well -- has likely been contaminated by floodwater mixing with sewage. Three children and two elderly patients are severely dehydrated. Your ORS supplies are running low, and the nearest supply depot is flooded. This is a potential cholera outbreak, and it could spread rapidly if not contained. The Sub-District Hospital has sent word that they too are overwhelmed.
rounds.goal: Manage a mass outbreak with limited supplies while implementing containment measures to prevent further spread.

choices.label: Triage Patients + Make Homemade ORS Solution
choices.feedback: You triage patients by severity and teach families to make WHO-recommended ORS at home: 1 litre boiled water + 6 teaspoons sugar + half teaspoon salt. This simple solution has saved millions of lives worldwide. India's ORS-zinc programme reduced diarrhoeal deaths in children by over 50%. The formula was popularized in India during the 1971 Bangladesh refugee crisis. Your quick triage and homemade ORS ensure no patient dies while awaiting medical supplies.

choices.label: Shut Down Contaminated Well + Distribute Chlorine Tablets
choices.feedback: You work with the Gram Panchayat to immediately close the contaminated well and distribute chlorine tablets (Aquatab) from your emergency supplies. You set up an alternative water point using your PHC's hand pump. The Jal Jeevan Mission aims to provide safe piped water to every rural household by 2024. Water-borne diseases cause over 37 million cases annually in India. Addressing the source of contamination is as important as treating the patients -- this is the fundamental principle of epidemiology pioneered by John Snow.

choices.label: Report to IDSP + Request Emergency Medical Supplies
choices.feedback: You immediately report to the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) using the S-form (suspected outbreak form). The District Rapid Response Team (RRT) is activated. India's IDSP, established after the 2003 SARS scare, is designed for exactly these situations. Within hours, the RRT arrives with supplies, and the district lab confirms Vibrio cholerae. Systematic reporting triggers the public health machinery -- one doctor cannot fight an epidemic alone, but one doctor can activate the system that can.

rounds.title: Round 8: Reflecting on Rural Healthcare
rounds.story: After six months at the PHC, you receive two job offers: a lucrative position at a corporate hospital in Ahmedabad paying five times your current salary, and a promotion to Medical Officer at the upgraded Health and Wellness Centre in your village with a modest raise. Your patients, ASHA workers, and the village community have come to depend on you. Kamala (Raju's mother) says you are the first doctor who listened. The Gram Panchayat offers to name the PHC after you. But your student loan is heavy, your parents want you in the city, and the rural posting is challenging in ways no textbook prepared you for.
rounds.goal: Reflect on the purpose of medicine and decide your professional path, considering duty, personal needs, and systemic healthcare challenges.

choices.label: Stay in the Village and Build the Healthcare System
choices.feedback: You choose to stay, inspired by doctors like Dr. Abhay Bang and Dr. Rani Bang who transformed rural healthcare in Gadchiroli, Maharashtra. India needs 6 lakh more doctors in rural areas. Your decision to stay means 10,000 villagers continue to have a trained doctor. The National Rural Health Mission's goal was exactly this -- bringing healthcare to the last mile. Your presence prevents thousands of unnecessary referrals and saves lives that statistics will never fully capture.

choices.label: Take the City Hospital Job (Pay Off Loans, Help Parents)
choices.feedback: Your decision is understandable -- India's medical education costs are high, and personal financial security matters. The systemic problem is not individual doctors leaving rural areas but a healthcare system that does not incentivize them to stay. India's 75% of healthcare infrastructure is in cities serving 30% of the population. Policy solutions include rural service bonds, higher rural salaries, and telemedicine bridges. You promise to return as a consultant and mentor future rural doctors.

choices.label: Propose a Hybrid Model: City Practice + Weekly Village Clinic
choices.feedback: You negotiate a creative solution: work at the Ahmedabad hospital four days a week and run a specialist clinic at the village PHC every weekend. You also set up a telemedicine link for emergencies. This hybrid model is increasingly adopted across India. Organizations like the Rural India Health Foundation connect urban specialists with rural communities. Your model could be replicated across Gujarat. Innovation in healthcare delivery -- not just in medicine -- is what India desperately needs.

choices.label: Train Local Health Workers Before Making Any Decision
choices.feedback: Before deciding, you spend a month conducting intensive training for ASHA workers, ANMs, and community volunteers. You create simple diagnostic protocols in Gujarati, stock the pharmacy, and establish referral pathways. Even if you leave, the system you build will sustain. This mirrors the approach of SEWA (Self Employed Women's Association) in Gujarat -- building community capacity that outlasts individual leaders. The most impactful doctors are not just healers but teachers and system-builders.

glossary_terms.definition: The first point of contact for rural healthcare in India, typically serving a population of 20,000-30,000. Staffed by a medical officer and supporting staff, PHCs provide preventive, promotive, and curative healthcare. Under Ayushman Bharat, many are being upgraded to Health and Wellness Centres.

Accredited Social Health Activist -- a trained female community health worker serving as a bridge between the village and the health system. India has nearly 10 lakh ASHA workers who facilitate immunisation, maternal care, and health awareness at the grassroots level.

India's flagship public health scheme launched in 2018 with two components: Health and Wellness Centres for comprehensive primary care, and Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY) providing health insurance of 5 lakh rupees per family per year for secondary and tertiary care.

A simple, life-saving solution of clean water, sugar, and salt that treats dehydration from diarrhoea. The WHO-recommended formula has saved tens of millions of lives globally. It was extensively deployed in India during the 1971 cholera epidemic among Bangladesh refugees.

Launched in 2005 to provide accessible, affordable, and quality healthcare to rural populations. It strengthened the public health infrastructure, deployed ASHA workers, and improved maternal and child health outcomes. Now subsumed under the National Health Mission (NHM).

cultural_context: India's healthcare system faces unique pressures — with a doctor-patient ratio far below WHO recommendations and a growing burden of lifestyle diseases. Dr. Patel's Clinic: Diagnosis Challenge builds the analytical and decision-making skills needed by India's future health leaders.
coaching_moment: Knowing when to take a risk and when to play safe is one of the most important life skills.

questions.question: What is 'empathy'?
questions.explanation: Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of others.

questions.question: A good leader should:

choices.text: Listen to the team and consider different views

questions.explanation: Good leaders listen to diverse perspectives before making informed decisions.

questions.question: What does 'delayed gratification' mean?

choices.text: Waiting for a bigger reward instead of taking a smaller one now

questions.explanation: Delayed gratification means resisting a smaller immediate reward for a larger future one.
